questions.question: In elliptic-curve cryptography, what is an isogeny (informally)?
options: A group homomorphism between elliptic curves with a finite kernel
A hash function from curve points to integers mod p
A proof that two curves have the same number of points
A constant-time algorithm for scalar multiplication
questions.explanation: An isogeny is a non-constant morphism that is also a group homomorphism; it is determined by a finite kernel.

questions.question: Why does this lesson use a tiny prime field (like p=419) instead of real CSIDH parameters?
options: So we can implement and test the math without external libraries and huge runtimes
Because CSIDH is only defined for small primes
Because large primes make elliptic curves stop forming a group
So that we can ignore key validation and side channels safely in production
questions.explanation: Toy parameters let you see and test the full pipeline (points, torsion, Vélu) in seconds; they do not imply production safety.

questions.question: In the short Weierstrass model y^2 = x^3 + ax + b over F_p, what does it mean for a point P to have order ℓ?
options: ℓP = O and for any 0 < k < ℓ, kP != O
P has x-coordinate equal to ℓ mod p
P is a point whose y-coordinate is a quadratic residue
The curve has exactly ℓ points total
questions.explanation: Order ℓ means P generates a cyclic subgroup of size ℓ: multiplying by ℓ gives the identity, and no smaller positive multiple does.

questions.question: What is the input that Vélu’s formulas need in order to construct an ℓ-isogeny E -> E/⟨P⟩ (odd prime ℓ) in this lesson?
options: A generator P of a cyclic kernel subgroup of order ℓ
Only the j-invariant of E
A discrete logarithm oracle for E(F_p)
A pairing e(P,Q) on E
questions.explanation: Vélu constructs the quotient curve and rational maps from the kernel subgroup; for a cyclic kernel, a generator P is enough.

questions.question: In the toy demo, why do the two quotient orders (first 3-isogeny then 5-isogeny vs first 5 then 3) produce the same j-invariant?
options: Because we transport the remaining torsion point through the isogeny map before taking the next quotient
Because all elliptic curves over F_p have the same j-invariant
Because j-invariants are always 0 in characteristic p
Because isogenies always commute without any additional structure
questions.explanation: Order-independence here relies on taking quotients by coprime-order kernels and mapping the other subgroup across via the isogeny.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the security warning in the lesson?
options: Correct math on toy parameters does not imply constant-time or production-safe cryptography
If code passes unit tests, it is safe to deploy in production
Side channels only matter on client devices, not servers
Isogeny-based cryptography is always safer than ECDH
questions.explanation: Production security requires constant-time implementations, validation, hardened failure behavior, and vetted parameters; toy correctness is not enough.

questions.question: Attack mindset: what is a realistic risk if an implementation accepts malformed public keys and then runs secret-dependent branches while processing them?
options: The attacker can use timing/cache behavior to learn information about the secret
The attacker can force p to become composite
The attacker can make the Legendre symbol return a wrong value mathematically
The attacker can always solve discrete logs instantly
questions.explanation: Malformed inputs can trigger exceptional cases and secret-dependent control flow; side-channel leakage can reveal bits of the secret over many queries.

questions.question: What does comparing j-invariants tell you in this lesson’s commute demo?
options: Whether two curves are isomorphic over an algebraic closure (a useful equivalence signal for the demo)
Whether two points are equal on the same curve
Whether the curve has prime order
Whether Vélu’s formulas ran in constant time
questions.explanation: Equal j-invariant indicates the curves are in the same isomorphism class over an algebraic closure; it’s a convenient check for this toy example.
